ai.definition: Bioprinting vascularised tissue involves using a combination of living cells and biocompatible materials to create three-dimensional structures that include blood vessel networks. These vessels are necessary for the survival of thicker tissues by providing nutrients and removing waste products.
ai.howItWorks: Cells and sacrificial inks (biomaterials) are co-printed layer by layer, forming a structure with channels. After printing, the sacrificial material is removed through a flushing process, leaving behind hollow channels that can be filled with blood vessels to create perfusable tissue structures.
ai.problemSolved: The main challenge in creating thick engineered tissues is ensuring they receive adequate nutrients and oxygenation. Vascularisation addresses this by integrating functional blood vessel networks within the printed tissue, enabling it to grow larger without necrosis (tissue death).
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves precise control over cell placement and material deposition using bioprinters. The process requires a sterile environment and careful calibration of printing parameters.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the tissue structure, selecting appropriate cells and biomaterials, preparing the bio-ink, printing the layers, and post-processing steps such as removing sacrificial materials and culturing the printed tissues.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the high cost of bioprinters, specialized cell lines, and advanced biomaterials. Additionally, the complexity of the process and the need for a controlled environment increase costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but still in early stages, with significant potential for breakthroughs in drug testing and regenerative medicine.
ai.regulation: Regulatory frameworks are emerging but not yet fully established. Current guidelines focus on the use of cells and tissues in medical applications, which may need to be adapted as bioprinting technologies advance.
ai.risks: Bioprinting risks include contamination, failure of the vascular network, and ethical concerns related to the use of living cells in manufacturing processes.
ai.profitability: Profitability is not yet established due to the early stage of development and high costs. However, potential future markets could include personalized medicine, drug discovery, and tissue engineering for clinical applications.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments may involve improvements in bioprinter technology, the use of stem cells, and the integration of more complex vascular networks to support larger tissues.

glossary.def: A process that uses a printer to deposit living cells and biomaterials to create three-dimensional tissue structures.
Tissue containing functional blood vessels, enabling it to receive nutrients and remove waste products effectively.
Biocompatible materials used in bioprinting that are later removed to create channels for vascularisation.

subsystems.name: Bioink formulation
subsystems.role: Provides living cells and a supportive matrix that can be printed and then crosslinked into a solid tissue.

subsystems.name: Sacrificial vascular ink
subsystems.role: Creates a network of channels that are later flushed out to become perfusable blood vessels.

subsystems.name: Printing system
subsystems.role: Deposits multiple materials layer by layer with precise spatial control.

subsystems.name: Endothelialisation and perfusion
subsystems.role: Lines the channels with endothelial cells and pumps oxygenated medium through them to keep the tissue alive.

subsystems.name: Imaging and control
subsystems.role: Verifies channel geometry, cell distribution, and tissue structure during and after printing.

subsystems.name: Support matrix and tissue cells
subsystems.role: The actual organ-specific cells and structural scaffold that give the tissue its function.

buildSteps.title: Design the tissue and vascular tree
buildSteps.detail: Use computer-aided design to model the organ shape and a branching vascular network, ensuring no cell is more than 200 µm from a channel — the approximate diffusion limit for oxygen.

buildSteps.title: Prepare the bioinks
buildSteps.detail: Mix tissue-specific cells with a hydrogel precursor. Separately prepare a sacrificial ink, such as Pluronic F127, that liquefies when cooled to around 4 °C.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate the printer
buildSteps.detail: Set extrusion pressure, print speed, and nozzle temperature so that both the cell-laden ink and the sacrificial ink deposit as continuous, uniform filaments.

buildSteps.title: Print the construct
buildSteps.detail: Alternate layers of cell-laden bioink and sacrificial ink, building a 3D block of tissue with an embedded network of channels that mimic blood vessels.

buildSteps.title: Crosslink the matrix
buildSteps.detail: Apply light or a chemical crosslinker to solidify the cell-laden hydrogel while leaving the sacrificial ink intact and removable.

buildSteps.title: Remove the sacrificial ink
buildSteps.detail: Cool the construct to liquefy the sacrificial ink, then flush it out with a warm buffer to leave hollow, interconnected channels.

buildSteps.title: Seed endothelial cells
buildSteps.detail: Perfuse a suspension of endothelial cells through the channels so they adhere to the walls and form a confluent, blood-compatible lining.

buildSteps.title: Perfuse and mature
buildSteps.detail: Connect the construct to a bioreactor that pumps oxygenated nutrient medium through the channels. Culture for days to weeks to allow the tissue to mature and stabilise.

buildSteps.title: Test and analyse
buildSteps.detail: Assess cell viability, vessel integrity, and tissue-specific function using microscopy and biochemical assays before the model is used for research or drug testing.

prerequisites.why: Needed to deposit multiple materials with the spatial control required to build a branching vascular network.
Provide a printable, cell-friendly matrix that can be crosslinked into a stable tissue scaffold.
Understanding how to line channels with endothelial cells that resist clotting and form tight junctions is essential for functional vessels.
Keeps nutrient medium flowing through the channels, which is the only way to keep cells beyond a few hundred micrometres alive.
Capillaries are 5–10 µm wide, but most bioprinters currently struggle to reliably create channels that small.
Thick tissues require weeks of sterile, stable perfusion without contamination or structural degradation.

pathway.milestone: Print vascularised tissue models up to a few millimetres thick for drug toxicity testing.
pathway.unlocks: More predictive drug screening and a reduction in animal testing.

pathway.milestone: Achieve capillary-scale channels (under 10 µm) with stable perfusion for several weeks, enabling tissues thicker than 1 cm.
pathway.unlocks: Functional organ models for research and early transplantation studies.

pathway.milestone: Integrate multiple cell types, including immune cells, to mimic organ complexity and disease states.
pathway.unlocks: Advanced disease modelling and personalised medicine approaches.

pathway.milestone: Implantable vascularised tissues (e.g., skin, blood vessel patches) that connect to a patient's own circulation.
pathway.unlocks: Regenerative therapies for organ failure and chronic wounds.

pathway.milestone: Whole organs (e.g., kidney, liver) grown from a patient's own cells with a complete vascular tree.
pathway.unlocks: An end to donor organ shortages and immune rejection.
